title: Beyond "Maus": How Tennessee's Schools Are Changing for the Better
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler argues that the headlines about Maus and book challenges in Tennessee hide a far more important story: the state is quietly rebuilding how it teaches reading. She explains that the standard approach conflicts with evidence on both decoding and comprehension, and that comprehension in particular depends on background knowledge that skills-focused instruction fails to build. She then documents the scale of Tennessee's response, from the Reading 360 screening and teacher-training programme to near-universal adoption of knowledge-building literacy curricula. She does not ignore the obstacles, notably the mismatch between a curriculum's content and the topics on standardised tests and the book challenges from a small, loud minority. She closes with practical fixes, such as community involvement in curriculum adoption, opt-out policies and alternative units, and a plea for journalists to cover classroom change rather than board-meeting drama.
points: Reading instruction has two evidence gaps, decoding (systematic phonics) and comprehension (knowledge and vocabulary), and most schools address neither well.

Tennessee paired a $100 million Reading 360 effort with training for 10,000 teachers and near-statewide use of knowledge-building curricula, an unusually fast curriculum shift for a local-control system.
A knowledge-building curriculum can clash with tests that are not tied to any body of knowledge, which makes district leaders nervous even though the payoff comes over years.
Book challenges look louder than they are: one Williamson County committee heard from just 37 people in a district of 17,000 elementary pupils, 23 of whom had no children there.
Suggested remedies include involving parents and board members in curriculum adoption, relying on opt-outs, and offering alternative units like Night in place of Maus.
quotes: If students from more affluent families struggle with decoding, they often get tutoring. And children from more educated families—who, in our society, are usually wealthier—are less likely to have comprehension problems because they pick up academic knowledge and vocabulary at home. But other kids rely on school for these things, and most schools haven’t been providing them effectively.

But evidence from cognitive science indicates that comprehension depends primarily on knowledge, either of the topic or of academic vocabulary in general. The subjects that could build that kind of knowledge—social studies, science, and the arts—have been squeezed out of the curriculum to make more time for practicing largely illusory comprehension skills.

Last summer the department provided two weeks of training in foundational literacy skills to 10,000 teachers in kindergarten through fifth grade, giving each a $1,000 stipend. Afterwards, 98% reported they felt equipped to teach reading more effectively.

Given how firmly ensconced the skills-focused approach to comprehension is throughout the country, this rapid uptake of a radically different kind of curriculum is nothing short of extraordinary. American school districts have a good deal of autonomy in choosing curriculum, so states generally need to rely on incentives and persuasion. Tennessee has clearly worked hard to help district officials and educators understand the need for change.

Despite all the publicity, the complaints could be coming from just a few loud parents. A committee in Williamson County that investigated challenges to the elementary curriculum there noted that—in a district with 17,000 students in kindergarten through fifth grade—it had received complaints from just 37 people, 23 of whom didn’t have children in the county’s elementary schools. (The committee removed only one of the books that were challenged.)

Currently, board members need to approve the choice, but they generally just rubber-stamp a decision made by a committee of educators. If only a few parents find a book objectionable, the best course of action might be to advise them to invoke the “opt-out” policies in place in most Tennessee school districts, which allow students to read an alternative text.
